question: What is the meaning of location in building in relation to physical composition?
description: In the context of building, location refers to the specific position or area within a building where a particular material or component is found. This is important for understanding the physical composition of the building, as different materials may be used in different locations based on their intended function, structural requirements, or aesthetic considerations. For example, the exterior walls of a building may be composed of different materials depending on their location, such as the metal cladding on the façade or the insulation material within the wall structure. Understanding the location of materials within a building is crucial for assessing the building's overall composition, structural integrity, and potential for reuse or recycling.

The aim 
of this assessment was to identify the material composition as accurate 
as possible by considering all elements of the building. Thereby the 
exterior walls were investigated in detail at one point of the building, 
where the metal cladding of the use case could be removed. From this 
punctual investigation it was assumed, that the composition of the 
exterior walls is the same. For the metal cladding, this assumption could 
be verified through the on-site inspection. The layer behind the cladding 
could only be verified through knocking. As the walls were assumed to 
compose of three layers, the third material could be verified from the 
interior. The same method was used for all building components, which 
were accessible (roof, foundation and interior walls). For the foundation 
some information could be obtained from the planning documents, 
though, the exact composition was obtained from drillings. However, 
not every building component was analyzed through destructive 
methods, thus, assumptions were made for some components. The 
masses of each component were calculated based on acquired thickness 
and area of each layer as well as the default material densities. 
The acquired information through the DA and UMA were docu­
mented in separate spreadsheets. 
2.4. Existing building (use case) 
The MP-method was tested on a real building, a lab and office facility 
of TU Wien (Fig. 2), allocated in the third district of Vienna. The typically 
industrial building has a total area of 1265 m2. The building consists of 
three parts: office, lab and storage, which can be distinguished from 
outside due to their different heights. The highest part of the building 
(storage) is 6,85 m high, whereas the lowest part (office) has a height of 
3,8 m. The load-bearing elements are mainly out of concrete and the 
insulation is out of mineral wool. The façade consists of a metal sheet 
cladding in a trapezoidal form. On the longest side the building has a 
length of about 62 m and on the widest side it has a width of about 24 m. 
M. Honic et al.
